# Proto-Gospel of James Chapter 23 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** P.Bodmer V / Greek MSS, Proto-Gospel of James 23 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/POX_023_page_001.jpg

---

## Chapter 23

**23:1** At the hour of the morning offering, the priests were standing ready, waiting for Zechariah to come and greet them with a blessing as was his custom — but he was long delayed. At last one of the priests had the courage to go in, and he saw congealed blood beside the altar of the Lord. And a voice said: "Zechariah has been slain, and his blood shall not be wiped away until his avenger comes."

**23:2** When he heard these words, he was afraid and went out and reported to the priests what he had seen and heard. And they had the courage to go in, and they saw what had happened. And the wainscotings of the temple cried out, and they rent their garments from the top to the bottom.

**23:3** And they searched for his body but found it not; but they found his blood turned to stone. And they were afraid and went out and told the people that Zechariah had been slain. And all the tribes of the people heard it and mourned him and lamented three days and three nights.

**23:4** And after three days the priests deliberated as to whom they should appoint in his place. And the lot fell to Simeon — for it was he to whom it had been revealed by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had seen the Christ in the flesh.

---

## Translator's Note

The discovery of the coagulated blood (23:1) and especially the blood "turned to stone" (23:3) are dramatic elaborations connecting Zechariah's death to the rhetoric of Genesis 4:10 ("your brother's blood cries out from the ground"). The three-day mourning (23:3) echoes the three days of Christ's death and resurrection — a typological parallel the author may intend. The appointment of Simeon (23:4) creates a narrative bridge to Luke 2:25-35 (Simeon's encounter with the infant Jesus at the temple), connecting the Protevangelium's timeline to the canonical Gospel infancy narrative.
